lessonTitle: Receiving Feedback and Reflecting on a Case Presentation

blocks.text: After presenting a patient on the ward round, a student hears the consultant say, 'That was too long and you missed the key negative.' The student's face flushes, and the first words out of his mouth are, 'Well, the team didn't tell me what you wanted.' The consultant nods, moves on, and the chance to learn has been lost.

blocks.markdown: Feedback is information about your performance given with the aim of improving it. Doctors receive it for the whole of their careers, from supervisors, peers, nurses and patients. The skill is not only to give a good presentation but to **use** the response to a presentation. This unit covers three skills: receiving feedback without defensiveness, turning it into **two specific points for improvement**, and recording **structured reflection** in a portfolio.

blocks.title: Feedback and reflection
blocks.text: Feedback is specific, descriptive information about performance given to help improve it. Reflection is the process of thinking about an experience, including your feelings and reasoning, to learn from it and decide what to do differently. Feedback supplies external information; reflection makes sense of it and plans action.

blocks.markdown:
### Receiving feedback without defensiveness

Defensiveness is a natural reaction when you feel judged, but it closes the conversation and discourages future feedback. Good receivers:

- **Listen to the end** without interrupting, and keep an open posture and eye contact.
- **Thank** the person for taking the time, even if the feedback is hard to hear.
- **Clarify** by asking for an example or for what the person would have wanted instead: 'Can you give me an example of what a shorter version would sound like?'
- **Avoid justification and blame**, such as 'I wasn't told' or 'it was a busy day'. You can offer context briefly later, if relevant, but only after understanding the feedback.
- **Summarise** what you have heard to check you have understood.
- **Reflect** afterwards on what is useful. You do not have to accept every point, but you should consider it carefully.

rows: 'That's not what I was told to do.'
'Thank you. Can you show me what you would have wanted me to say?'
Interrupting or arguing during the feedback
Waiting until the person has finished before responding
Blaming the situation or the team
Describing what you will do differently next time
Dismissing the feedback as the observer's opinion
Asking for specific examples to understand it
Summarising the points and agreeing a next step
blocks.caption: Defensive and open responses to feedback.

blocks.title: Responding to critical feedback
blocks.prompt: A registrar tells you after your presentation: 'You spoke for five minutes and I lost track of the main problem. You started with the family history before the presenting complaint.' How do you respond?

steps.text: Listen to the entire comment without interrupting and do not rush to explain. Notice any feeling of embarrassment but do not act on it.
Thank the registrar: 'Thank you for telling me, that is useful.'
Clarify: 'Could you tell me where you would have wanted me to start, and what you would have left out?' This turns a criticism into concrete guidance.
Summarise: 'So I should open with a one-line summary and the presenting complaint, shorten the background, and bring the family history in only if it is relevant.' Check that the registrar agrees.

blocks.answer: Listen, thank, clarify with examples, and summarise what you will change, rather than explaining or defending the earlier version.

blocks.markdown:
### Identifying two specific points for improvement

Feedback is only useful if you act on it. After a presentation, pick **two** points to improve, not ten. Choose points that are:

- **Specific**: 'my presenting complaint was lost in the middle of a long history' is better than 'be clearer'.
- **Actionable**: it names something you can practise ('start with a one-line summary').
- **Observable**: someone could see whether you did it next time.
- **Prioritised**: choose the points that would make the biggest difference.

It can help to include **one thing you did well to keep doing**, because strengths should also be kept. Write the points down as soon as possible after the presentation, while the feedback is fresh.

blocks.title: From comments to two improvement points
blocks.prompt: You receive these comments after presenting a patient with abdominal pain: 'Good eye contact; a lot of detail but disorganised; forgot to mention the patient's allergies; spoke too quietly; the plan was clear.' Choose two points for improvement and one strength.

steps.text: Sort the comments into strengths (eye contact, clear plan) and weaknesses (disorganised detail, omitted allergies, quiet voice).
Prioritise by effect on patient care and the audience's understanding: leaving out allergies is a safety omission, and disorganised detail undermines the structure of the presentation.

Write them as specific, actionable points: (1) 'Follow the standard order of history, examination, impression and plan, including drug history and allergies every time.' (2) 'Use a one-line summary at the start, and trim detail so that key facts are easy to follow.'
Note one strength to maintain: 'Clear, well-organised plan and good eye contact.' The quiet voice can be a later goal once the first two are addressed.

blocks.answer: Two points: include allergies and drug history routinely, and open with a one-line summary with trimmed detail; keep the clear plan and eye contact as a strength.

blocks.markdown:
### Recording structured reflection in a portfolio

A portfolio is a record of learning used throughout training and by the GMC and medical schools to show development. A good entry uses a **structured model** to move from description to learning to action, rather than simply describing what happened. Two models are widely used:

- **Rolfe's model**: **What?** (what happened), **So what?** (what did I learn, feel, think; why did it matter), **Now what?** (what will I do differently).
- **Gibbs' reflective cycle**: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan.

Regardless of the model, a reflective entry should be honest, linked to evidence (including the feedback), end with a concrete action plan, and **protect confidentiality**: do not include patient names, dates of birth, hospital numbers or other identifying details.

rows: 'I presented a patient with chest pain to the consultant and received feedback that it was too long.'
'I felt embarrassed, but I realised I did not prioritise relevant details and had not practised.'
Specific actions and a review date
'I will rehearse with a one-line summary and a three-minute limit and ask for feedback on my next two presentations.'
blocks.caption: Applying Rolfe's model to a reflective entry.

items: Write reflections soon after the event.
Include your feelings and your reasoning, not only the facts.
End with a specific action and a way to check it was done.
Ask for feedback again later to see whether you have improved.

blocks.title: Feedback is a gift, not a verdict
blocks.text: Feedback describes a performance, not your worth as a person. Treating it as information to use, rather than as a judgement to defend against, is what allows trainees to improve quickly.

points: Receive feedback by listening fully, thanking, clarifying with examples and summarising, without justifying or blaming.
Choose two specific, actionable, observable points for improvement and keep one strength.
Record reflection in a structured model such as Rolfe's (What? So what? Now what?) or Gibbs' cycle.
Reflective entries end with a concrete action plan and must be anonymised to protect patient confidentiality.

questions.stem: A consultant tells a student, 'You didn't mention the patient's allergies.' Which response best shows receiving feedback without defensiveness?

options.text: 'Thank you, I missed that. I'll include drug history and allergies every time.'
'I was never told to include them.'
'The patient didn't say they had any.'
'I think that is unfair.'

questions.correctOptionText: 'Thank you, I missed that. I'll include drug history and allergies every time.'

distractorRationale.a: Correct: acknowledges the point and commits to change.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: justifies the omission instead of accepting feedback.

questions.explanation: Open responses acknowledge the feedback and move towards action. Justifying, blaming or dismissing closes the conversation and wastes the opportunity to learn.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most useful way to respond when feedback is vague, such as 'your presentation was disorganised'?

options.text: Ask for a specific example of where it became disorganised and what a better version would look like
Ignore it because it is not detailed
Argue that it was well organised
Apologise repeatedly

questions.correctOptionText: Ask for a specific example of where it became disorganised and what a better version would look like

distractorRationale.a: Correct: clarifying turns vague feedback into something actionable.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: excessive apology does not clarify the problem.

questions.explanation: Asking for examples makes feedback concrete and usable. It also shows that you value the comment and want to improve.

questions.stem: After a ward-round presentation a student receives eight comments. According to the approach in this lesson, what is the best next step?

options.text: Choose two specific, actionable priority points and keep one strength
Try to fix all eight at once
Pick the one that is easiest to ignore
Wait to see whether anyone repeats the comments

questions.correctOptionText: Choose two specific, actionable priority points and keep one strength

distractorRationale.a: Correct: prioritise a manageable number of changes.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: too many changes at once reduces success.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: avoids the points that need work.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: passive and unlikely to lead to change.

questions.explanation: Focusing on two prioritised points makes improvement achievable and trackable. Retaining one strength also acknowledges what to keep doing.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best-worded improvement point?

options.text: Open each presentation with a one-line summary containing age, sex, presenting problem and duration
Be better
Try harder
Do not make mistakes

questions.correctOptionText: Open each presentation with a one-line summary containing age, sex, presenting problem and duration
questions.explanation: A useful improvement point states a specific behaviour that can be practised and observed by someone else next time.

questions.stem: In Rolfe's reflective model, which question asks the writer to decide on future actions?

options.text: Now what?
What?
So what?
Why not?

distractorRationale.d: Wrong: not part of the model.

questions.explanation: Rolfe's model has three questions: what happened, so what (learning and feelings), and now what (action). The last turns reflection into change.

questions.stem: A student writes in her portfolio: 'Mr Ahmed, DOB 4 May 1952, hospital number 123456, was a difficult patient to present because...'. What is the main problem with this entry?

options.text: It contains patient-identifiable information, which breaches confidentiality
It uses a structured model
It is too short
It includes feelings

questions.correctOptionText: It contains patient-identifiable information, which breaches confidentiality

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: use of a model is encouraged.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: length is not the main issue.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: feelings are an expected part of reflection.

questions.explanation: Portfolio entries must not contain names, dates of birth or hospital numbers. Anonymising protects the patient and is a professional requirement.

questions.stem: Explaining why a mistake happened, immediately after feedback is given, is the best way to show you are receptive to it.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Explaining or justifying immediately can sound defensive and may stop the feedback. It is better to listen, thank and clarify first, offering context only briefly and later if relevant.

questions.stem: A student is told after a case presentation, 'Your history was too detailed and I couldn't tell what you thought was wrong.' Describe how the student should respond in the conversation and what they should write down afterwards.
markingGuide: Asks for an example or what they would have preferred
Records two specific, actionable points such as a one-line summary and stating a working diagnosis
questions.explanation: The conversation should be receptive and clarifying, and the written points should be specific and manageable. This turns critical comments into a plan for improving the next presentation.

questions.stem: Using Rolfe's model, write a short portfolio reflection on receiving feedback that your case presentation was too long. Explain why the entry must be anonymised.
markingGuide: What?: brief factual description of the presentation and feedback
So what?: feelings, analysis and learning, for example why it was too long
Now what?: a specific action such as rehearsal and a three-minute limit, with a plan to check
Entry is honest and links to the feedback
Confidentiality is a professional duty and portfolios may be seen by others
questions.explanation: A structured reflection moves from description to learning to a concrete plan. Anonymising protects patient confidentiality because portfolios can be read by supervisors and assessors.

questions.stem: A student is given the feedback 'Good structure, but you forgot the examination findings and spoke very fast.' Which pair of improvement points is best formed?

options.text: Include examination findings every time, and practise speaking more slowly with pauses between sections
Be more confident and be better prepared
Speak well and do not forget things
Present less often

questions.correctOptionText: Include examination findings every time, and practise speaking more slowly with pauses between sections

distractorRationale.a: Correct: two specific actionable points from the feedback.

questions.explanation: Specific points name behaviours that can be changed and observed. They also correspond to the two weaknesses in the feedback rather than general advice.
